reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / RCOG postpartum haemorrhage and emergency obstetrics guidance
clinicalPearls: Uterine inversion is the turning inside-out of the uterine fundus through the cervix, most often as an acute complication of the third stage of labour
It classically presents with sudden severe lower abdominal pain, haemorrhage, and shock that appears disproportionate to visible blood loss
A key contributor is excessive cord traction or fundal pressure before placental separation, particularly with a relaxed uterus
On examination the fundus may be absent from the abdomen and a mass may be palpable or visible at the introitus or in the vagina
Profound, partly neurogenic (vagally mediated) shock is characteristic and may be out of proportion to bleeding
Immediate management is resuscitation and prompt manual replacement of the uterus, ideally before a constriction ring forms
Uterine relaxation with a tocolytic or anaesthetic agent can facilitate replacement, after which uterotonics are given to restore tone
If manual replacement fails, hydrostatic techniques or surgical repositioning are required
reference.pathophysiology: Uterine inversion occurs when the fundus descends and passes through the dilated cervix, typically when an atonic or partially relaxed uterus is subjected to traction on the cord or pressure on the fundus while the placenta remains adherent, especially with a fundal placental site. The inverted uterus and its attachments produce intense stimulation of pelvic autonomic nerves, causing a vagally mediated component to the shock alongside haemorrhage from the placental bed. A constriction ring may form at the cervix, trapping the inverted fundus and making replacement progressively harder, which is why speed of recognition and relaxation of the uterus are central to management.
additionalDifferentials: Large prolapsing uterine or submucosal fibroid
Other causes of postpartum collapse such as major haemorrhage or sepsis
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination confirming absence of the fundus abdominally and a vaginal or introital mass
Full blood count and coagulation studies
Group and crossmatch with activation of major haemorrhage support
Continuous monitoring of vital signs and urine output
Ultrasound if the diagnosis is uncertain and time permits
Assessment for retained placenta once the uterus is replaced
redFlags: Postpartum collapse with shock disproportionate to visible blood loss
A fundal mass at the introitus or in the vagina with an absent abdominal fundus
Failed manual replacement or formation of a tight constriction ring
Ongoing haemorrhage after repositioning suggesting atony or retained placenta
reference.prognosis: With immediate recognition, resuscitation, and prompt replacement, most women recover fully. Delay increases the risk of severe haemorrhage, prolonged shock, need for surgery, and, rarely, hysterectomy or maternal death.
pitfalls: Applying cord traction or fundal pressure before placental separation, precipitating inversion
Attributing profound shock solely to blood loss and missing the neurogenic component
Delaying replacement so that a constriction ring forms and prevents manual reduction
Removing an adherent placenta before replacing the uterus, worsening haemorrhage
management: Immediate call for help with aggressive resuscitation for the combined haemorrhagic and neurogenic shock using intravenous fluids and blood products
Prompt manual replacement of the fundus by the Johnson manoeuvre before a constriction ring forms, leaving an adherent placenta in situ until after replacement
Uterine relaxation with tocolytics or volatile anaesthetic agents to facilitate replacement
Uterotonics such as oxytocin, ergometrine and prostaglandins once replaced, to restore tone and prevent re-inversion
Hydrostatic replacement by the O'Sullivan technique or surgical replacement if manual reduction fails
Manual removal of the retained placenta after the uterus is repositioned
Activation of the major haemorrhage protocol with senior obstetric and anaesthetic support
